reason: The court held that a mistake or oversight by the party or attorney was not a cause outside control for relief under section 765.
The court decided the narrower section 765 late-appeal point, not a general rule about being excused from responsibility.
The court treated genuine and lawful reasonable cause for six-month absence as the statutory protection against ejectment under section 28.
This is a case-specific evidential finding about whether the landlord was informed, not a ratio-level legal rule.
The court found no exclusive possession by dependents on these facts because outsiders were present, not that dependents generally lack exclusive possession.
The statement drops the vital last-will and suspicious-circumstances limitation on the exception to the ordinary burden under section 101.
The observation concerned reading the trial judgment as a whole on the EQD issue and was not a rule construing Evidence Ordinance section 101.
The point was material only because the agreement and appropriation questions were disputed facts unsuitable for writ proceedings.
The statement omits the material limitation that non-interference was in writ proceedings where the issue depended solely on disputed facts.
The court set aside the injunction because acquisition by the State meant the plaintiff had no prima facie case.
The court relied on the exceptional-circumstances threshold to exercise revision despite the unavailed appeal remedy.
The court held that the injunction order caused a miscarriage of justice and therefore justified revisionary intervention.
The court applied the rule that an owner who landlocks himself by his own act cannot claim a way of necessity over a neighbour's land.
The retained outlet over the front portion was central to the holding that subdivision cannot impose a servitude on neighbours.
The court used Chapter XXXVIII's testamentary procedure and purpose as the basis for requiring the deposited will to be proved or rejected.
The actual holding was limited to not dismissing testamentary proceedings merely because a section 517 probate application was withdrawn after a will was deposited.
This is a factual finding about the plan and deeds in this partition case rather than a legal ratio.
The statement overstates the court's qualified wording that proof of original ownership is not always placed at a very high degree.
The court rejected the 50-year-use finding as insufficient and required adverse prescriptive user, so the statement reverses the point.
The wording records the trial judge's factual error in this appeal, not a standalone legal rule on ways of necessity.
The court held only that deed invalidation and declaration of title were not misjoined and were effectively one cause, not that any multiple causes may be raised.
The fraud corroboration proposition is supported, but Civil Procedure Code section 35(1) was not the provision construed for that rule.
The actual rule concerns civil fraud on a balance of probabilities with stricter proof for serious imputations, and section 35(1) is the wrong statute field.
The statement omits the material exceptions that genuineness may be impeached by an adverse claimant or proof may be required by the court.
The court's partition-law holding displaced the ordinary Evidence Ordinance subscribing-witness rule where the later Partition Law applies.
